claude.sample_unit: evaluations of LLM-generated instructions by 62 primary health care prescribers

links.outcome: Effect of retrieval-augmented generation on instruction quality and errors versus Llama3.1-8B without RAG
links.effect: RAG raised median overall score (79.9 vs 66.5; P=.44 vs base), reduced contradictory/vague errors (16.7% vs 34.8%) and factual errors (7.6% vs 15.2%), but hallucination (9.1% vs 13.6%) and incorrect-use errors (22.8% each) were similar.
links.quote: Llama3.1-8B-RAG had a lesser frequency of type 2 (n=11, 16.7%) and type 3 (n=5, 7.6%) errors compared to Llama3.1-8B without RAG, type 2 (n=23, 34.8%) and type 3 (n=10, 15.2%) errors.

links.outcome: Frequency of errors and hallucinations in LLM-generated medication instructions
links.effect: Instructions leading to incorrect use in 22.7% (ChatGPT-4.0), 22.8% (Llama3.1-8B), 22.8% (Llama3.1-8B-RAG); hallucination 10.6%, 13.6%, 9.1%.
links.quote: The number of errors identified in the instructions generated by the models demonstrated the necessity for human oversight of the technology, which is expected in PHC settings in alignment with principles for the ethical and responsible use of AI [ 9 ].

links.outcome: Output accuracy and safety of LLM medication instructions rated by clinicians
links.effect: About 22.7% of instructions per model could lead to incorrect medication use; Llama3.1-8B scored lower than ChatGPT-4.0 on adequacy (5.39 vs 6.82).
links.quote: Instructions leading to incorrect use of the medication had similar frequency among the models(ChatGPT-4.0: n=15, 22.7%; Llama3.1-8B: n=19, 22.8%; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: n=19, 22.8%; chi-square test P=.71).

links.outcome: Language simplification of LLM patient instructions rated by prescribers
links.effect: ChatGPT-4.0 language simplification mean 7.05 vs Llama3.1-8B-RAG 5.44 (P<.001) and Llama3.1-8B 5.41; RAG did not improve simplification.
links.quote: ChatGPT-4.0 received higher scores in the language simplification criterion than Llama3.1-8B-RAG (mean 7.05, SD 1.5 vs mean 5.44, SD 2.6; post hoc test P<.001).

links.outcome: Verification of differential effects of instructions across patient literacy groups
links.effect: Study did not verify differential effects across patient groups with varying educational level, culture, age, or health literacy.
links.quote: We state the lack of verification regarding differential effects on the instructions across groups of patients with varying educational levels, cultural aspects, age or health literacy, which demands further attention.

unlisted_practices: Use of open-source locally run LLMs for privacy versus proprietary models
Weighted, System Usability Scale-derived human evaluation scale with alternating positive/negative items

links.effect: Overall scores differed: ChatGPT 88.4, Llama 66.5, Llama-RAG 79.9; Kruskal-Wallis P=.003.
links.quote: The 3 models yielded high overall scores for producing qualified instructions (ChatGPT-4.0: median 88.4, IQR 22.8; Llama3.1-8B: median 66.5, IQR 50.9; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: median 79.9, IQR 34.4; Kruskal-Wallis test P=.003).

links.effect: Type1/type4 errors similar across models (P=.71/P=.67); RAG had lower type2/type3 than no RAG: 16.7%/7.6% vs 34.8%/15.2%.
links.quote: Regarding the presence or absence of errors, the 3 models were similar in terms of error type 1 (chi-square test P =.71), and type 4 (chi-square test P =.67), as presented in Table 5 .

links.effect: Incorrect-use instructions: ChatGPT n=15 (22.7%), Llama n=19 (22.8%), Llama-RAG n=19 (22.8%); P=.71.
links.quote: Instructions leading to incorrect use of the medication had similar frequency among the models(ChatGPT-4.0: n=15, 22.7%; Llama3.1-8B: n=19, 22.8%; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: n=19, 22.8%; chi-square test P=.71).

links.effect: Language simplification: ChatGPT mean 7.05 (SD 1.5) vs Llama-RAG 5.44 (SD 2.6); P<.001.
links.quote: ChatGPT-4.0 received higher scores in the language simplification criterion than Llama3.1-8B-RAG (mean 7.05, SD 1.5 vs mean 5.44, SD 2.6; post hoc test P<.001).

links.effect: Hallucinations: ChatGPT n=7 (10.6%), Llama n=9 (13.6%), Llama-RAG n=6 (9.1%); P=.67.
links.quote: The frequencies of hallucination were similar (ChatGPT-4.0: n=7, 10.6%; Llama3.1-8B: n=9, 13.6%; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: n=6, 9.1%; chi-square test P=.67).

links.outcome: errors and quality of instructions with retrieval-augmented generation
links.effect: Llama3.1-8B-RAG had fewer contradictory (16.7% vs 34.8%) and factual errors (7.6% vs 15.2%) than Llama3.1-8B, but similar overall scores (P=.44), incorrect use errors (22.8% vs 22.8%), and hallucinations (9.1% vs 13.6%).
links.quote: Llama3.1-8B-RAG had a lesser frequency of type 2 (n=11, 16.7%) and type 3 (n=5, 7.6%) errors compared to Llama3.1-8B without RAG, type 2 (n=23, 34.8%) and type 3 (n=10, 15.2%) errors.

screen.practice: retrieval-augmented generation grounding on patient information leaflets
screen.reason: The study empirically tests whether adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using patient information leaflets to an open-source LLM improves performance, adequacy, and hallucination rates in medication instructions compared to base models, evaluated by 62 healthcare professionals.
